# Optical modules and a reusable cache {#sec-modules-cache}

Everything so far assumed an ideal detector: a point, isotropically
sensitive, fully efficient. A real optical module (OM) is none of those. This
chapter removes the second assumption exactly, and shows that doing so costs
one change of a right-hand side — after which a single stored solve answers
for an entire detector array.

## The acceptance is the right-hand side {#sec-om-acceptance}

Let the module have an angular acceptance $A(\mathbf s)$: the probability,
relative to head-on, that a photon arriving with direction $\mathbf s$ is
registered. The quantity measured is no longer $\int I\,\mathrm d\Omega$ but

$$
K_A(\mathbf r,t;\mathbf s_0)=\int_{S^2}A(\mathbf s)\,I(\mathbf r,\mathbf s,t)
\,\mathrm d\Omega .
$$ {#eq-om-measured}

Run the reciprocity argument of @sec-adjoint again, changing nothing except
the function paired against $\tilde I$. With $L=D-V$ and the bilinear pairing,

$$
\tilde K_A=\langle A,L^{-1}\delta(\cdot-\mathbf s_0)\rangle
=\langle L^{-1}A,\delta(\cdot-\mathbf s_0)\rangle
=\bigl[L^{-1}A\bigr](\mathbf s_0),
$$

so that

$$
\boxed{(D-V)\,h_A=A,\qquad
\tilde K_A(\mathbf k,\omega;\mathbf s_0)=h_A(\mathbf s_0).}
$$ {#eq-om-adjoint}

This is @eq-adjoint-h with $1$ replaced by $A$, and $1$ is exactly the
acceptance of an isotropic detector of unit efficiency. The operator on the
left is untouched: **the matrix built in @sec-numerical-scheme does not
change at all**, neither its diagonal, nor its off-diagonals, nor its tail
closure. Only the vector on the right does. Every property that made the
matrix cheap — tridiagonal, exactly closed, independent of the source
direction — survives unchanged.

What does change is the symmetry. $1$ is axisymmetric about every axis;
$A$ is axisymmetric only about the module axis $\widehat{\mathbf n}$. Expanding
$A$ about that axis and applying the addition theorem in the
$\widehat{\mathbf k}$ frame,

$$
A(\widehat{\mathbf n}\cdot\mathbf s)=\sum_{l}\alpha_l
\sum_{m=-l}^{l}Y^*_{lm}(\widehat{\mathbf n})\,Y_{lm}(\mathbf s),
\qquad
\alpha_l=2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}A(x)P_l(x)\,\mathrm dx ,
$$ {#eq-om-alpha}

which carries $m\ne0$ unless $\widehat{\mathbf n}$ happens to align with
$\mathbf k$. This is the case @sec-method-choice flagged: a directional
*detector*, not a directional source, is what brings the azimuthal index
back. Since $D$ and $V$ both preserve $m$, the system stays block-diagonal,
one tridiagonal block per $m$ with couplings
$a^m_l=\sqrt{(l^2-m^2)/(4l^2-1)}$ — a bounded, well-defined extension rather
than a different method.

The normalization is fixed by the isotropic limit: $A\equiv1$ gives
$\alpha_0=4\pi$ and $\alpha_{l>0}=0$, which must reproduce the ideal detector
of @sec-setup. It does.

## An isotropic flash needs no new solve at all {#sec-om-isotropic}

For the one case this chapter actually computes — an isotropic flash, as a
diffuser-ball laser produces — the $m\ne0$ blocks never appear, and the
existing machinery is already enough.

The reason is that $\tilde I$ for an isotropic source is axisymmetric about
$\mathbf k$, since its source term is the constant $1/4\pi$. Its Legendre
coefficients about that axis are the $h_l$ already computed. The detector
acceptance is axisymmetric about $\widehat{\mathbf n}$. The overlap of two
axisymmetric functions about different axes is a Legendre series in the angle
between the axes,

$$
\tilde K_A(\mathbf k)=\sum_l \alpha_l\,\frac{h_l(k,\omega)}{4\pi}
\sqrt{\tfrac{2l+1}{2}}\;P_l(\widehat{\mathbf n}\cdot\widehat{\mathbf k}),
$$

and the plane-wave identity
$\int\mathrm d\Omega_{\widehat{\mathbf k}}\,e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}
P_l(\widehat{\mathbf n}\cdot\widehat{\mathbf k})
=4\pi i^lj_l(kr)P_l(\widehat{\mathbf n}\cdot\widehat{\mathbf r})$ then carries
it back to coordinate space:

$$
\boxed{
K_A(r,\omega)=\frac1{2\pi^2}\sum_{l=0}^{J}i^l\sqrt{\frac{2l+1}{2}}\,
\frac{\alpha_l}{4\pi}\,P_l(\cos\Theta)
\int_0^\infty k^2j_l(kr)\,h_l(k,\omega)\,\mathrm dk ,
}
$$ {#eq-om-multipole}

with $\cos\Theta=\widehat{\mathbf n}\cdot\widehat{\mathbf r}$ the cosine at
which the source-to-module line meets the module's head-on direction.

@eq-om-multipole is the same sum as @sec-spatial, with $P_l(\nu)$ replaced by
$\alpha_lP_l(\cos\Theta)/4\pi$. Two consequences follow immediately.

*One solve serves every module type.* The radial integrals do not know about
$A$. Computing them once and applying different $\alpha_l$ afterwards gives
the response of an ideal detector, of a real module, and of any hypothetical
module, at the cost of a contraction each.

*A smooth acceptance is cheap.* The sum runs only as far as $A$ has
coefficients. For $A(x)=(1+x)/2$ exactly two terms contribute; a bare cosine
$\max(x,0)$ has a kink and needs hundreds. The cost of a query therefore
measures the *angular bandwidth of the detector*, which is a satisfying thing
for a cost to measure.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Checks on eq-om-multipole"}
Three independent checks were run before this formula was used for anything.

Setting $\alpha_0=4\pi$ and $\alpha_{l>0}=0$ reproduces the solver's own
isotropic-source branch to $2\times10^{-14}$ in orders 0 and 1.

Weighting by $P_l(\nu)$ instead reproduces the solver's *directed*-source
result to $6\times10^{-14}$, which tests the shared radial integrals.

The angular identity behind it — $\int A(\widehat{\mathbf n}\cdot\mathbf s)
\tilde I(\widehat{\mathbf k}\cdot\mathbf s)\,\mathrm d\Omega$ equals the
Legendre series above — was checked at fixed $k$ against a direct
two-dimensional quadrature over the sphere on a $400\times400$ grid,
agreeing to $6\times10^{-13}$.
:::

Orders 0 and 1 need one remark each. The ballistic photon travels straight
from the flash, so it arrives exactly along $\widehat{\mathbf r}$ and its
weight is simply $A(\cos\Theta)$, evaluated from the acceptance itself rather
than from its truncated series — a point evaluation near a kink is exactly
where a truncated Legendre series rings. The first order is available two
ways: through the exact full-HG quadrature of @sec-coordinate-first, which
applies only to an isotropic detector, and through the finite-$L$ multipole
coefficients, which is what @eq-om-multipole needs. Their difference is a
property of $L$ and is measured, not assumed: at $L=64$ it is below
$10^{-6}$ of the first order itself out to $60\,\mathrm m$, and stays below
$1.3\times10^{-3}$ of the *total* charge everywhere in the cached range.

## What is not covered {#sec-om-limits}

A directed source read by a directional module is not implemented. It needs
the $m\ne0$ blocks of @sec-om-acceptance, and its spatial inversion no longer
collapses to a single $j_l$ sum, because the integrand then depends on
$\widehat{\mathbf k}$ through two independent directions. The result would be
a function of $r$ and three cosines rather than $r$ and one.

Nothing else here is an approximation of that case: the isotropic-flash
result of @eq-om-multipole is exact. The gap is a missing capability, not a
hidden error.

Also outside scope, and more mundane: the finite size of the module, shadowing
by its own hardware and by the string, the cable, the glass, and any
wavelength dependence within the flash. The module is still a point.

## A cache of multipole moments {#sec-cache}

@eq-om-multipole and the directed-source formula of @sec-spatial share
everything except their angular weights. What they share is worth storing:

$$
M_l(r,\omega)=\frac{i^l}{2\pi^2}\sqrt{\frac{2l+1}{2}}
\int_0^\infty k^2j_l(kr)\,h_l(k,\omega)\,\mathrm dk .
$$ {#eq-cache-moments}

`lighthit.cache` stores exactly these, for the first order and for the
$\ge2$ part, on a grid in $r$. A query contracts them against whichever
weights the detector calls for. Because the angular dependence is applied at
query time in closed form, it carries **no interpolation error at all**: the
only interpolated variable is distance.

The grid follows the constraint of @sec-discretizations that $J$ must track
$k_{\max}r$, so the cache is banded, each band carrying its own converged
settings. The bands used below, for the synthetic near-Baikal medium, were
fixed by the scan recorded in `docs/cache-baikal/report.json`:

| band | $k_{\max}$ | $J$ | radii | build |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| $10$–$20\,\mathrm m$ | $12$ | $364$ | 20 | $15\,\mathrm s$ |
| $20$–$60\,\mathrm m$ | $6$ | $526$ | 32 | $35\,\mathrm s$ |
| $60$–$400\,\mathrm m$ | $3$ | $1620$ | 50 | $175\,\mathrm s$ |

Building is dominated by the spherical Bessel tables, not by transport: the
angular solve is about $1\,\mathrm s$ of the total, because it is computed
once per frequency and shared by every radius. That is the same sharing
`PointGreenSolver` already does within one call, kept across calls.

Interpolation in distance uses a cubic spline in $\log r$ applied to the
moments divided by $e^{-\mu_ar}/4\pi r^2$, a smooth positive reference that
removes most of the dynamic range. Measured against exact solves at off-grid
geometry, with errors quoted relative to the total charge:

| band | median | maximum |
|---|---:|---:|
| $10$–$20\,\mathrm m$ | $2.9\times10^{-7}$ | $1.2\times10^{-5}$ |
| $20$–$60\,\mathrm m$ | $1.5\times10^{-6}$ | $1.1\times10^{-5}$ |
| $60$–$300\,\mathrm m$ | $5.9\times10^{-5}$ | $2.2\times10^{-1}$ |

The outlier in the far band is not an interpolation failure. It occurs where
the charge itself has fallen to $\sim10^{-16}$ per square metre per emitted
photon, and at that level the *exact* reference is not converged either:
changing $k_{\max}$ between $2$, $3$ and $4\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ moves it by tens
of percent (@sec-discretizations). The disagreement is below the method's own
floor, at signals around $10^{-4}$ photoelectrons.

## What a module is sensitive to {#sec-om-maps}

With the acceptance in the right-hand side, "what does this module see" is a
computation rather than an intuition. The cached moments answer it directly,
because they *are* the angular structure of the arriving light. Writing
$I(x)$ for the distribution of arrival directions at the module, with $x$
measured from the source-to-module line, the derivation above inverts to

$$
I(x)=\frac1{4\pi}\sum_l M_l\,P_l(x),
\qquad
\langle\cos\rangle=\frac{M_1}{3M_0},
$$ {#eq-arrival}

so the mean arrival cosine needs only the first two cached moments and no
truncation at all.

The result contradicts the intuition that multiple scattering isotropizes
light.

![Mean arrival cosine against distance, for singly and multiply scattered
light.](../cache-baikal/figures/arrival-mean-cos.png){#fig-arrival width=70%}

At every distance reached here the arriving light is strongly forward
directed: $\langle\cos\rangle$ is $0.959\to0.983$ for single scattering and
$0.893\to0.937$ for everything above it, against $g=0.9$ for a single
collision. Multiply scattered light arrives barely less directed than singly
scattered light.

The reason is a length scale. Deflection accumulates over the transport
length $1/[\mu_s(1-g)]$, which for this medium is
$$
\frac1{0.022\times(1-0.9)}=455\ \mathrm m ,
$$
while absorption removes light over $1/\mu_a=14.3\,\mathrm m$. Photons are
absorbed long before they can random-walk into isotropy, so at $r\ll455\,
\mathrm m$ the problem is quasi-ballistic, not diffusive — a regime where the
Green's function still carries direction. Note that this is *not* the same
statement as the orders being small: by $200\,\mathrm m$ the $\ge2$ component
carries most of the charge (@sec-baikal-laser). It carries it forward.

The consequence for a module is that its effective directionality is close to
its acceptance curve, order by order.

![Response of three module models against the angle to the source, split by
scattering order, at $r=60\,\mathrm m$. The dashed curve is the acceptance
$A(x)$ itself.](../cache-baikal/figures/om-angular-map.png){#fig-om-angular width=100%}

The ballistic order follows $A$ exactly — it must, arriving from one
direction. What @fig-om-angular shows is that the scattered orders very
nearly do too: each is a mildly broadened copy of the acceptance rather than
a flat pedestal. For the smooth $(1+x)/2$ module every order is exactly
linear in $\cos\Theta$, because that acceptance has only two Legendre
coefficients and @eq-om-multipole then has only two terms; the orders differ
only in slope. The one-sided $\max(x,0)$ module shows the effect that does
survive: below its cut-off it still collects a little light, entirely from the
scattered orders, because the arrival distribution has a tail even though its
mean is forward.

![Directional contrast against distance, for the three module
models.](../cache-baikal/figures/om-contrast.png){#fig-om-contrast width=100%}

So the concrete answer is the opposite of the diffusive expectation: in
Baikal-like water, over cluster-scale distances, a module remains sensitive
mainly to where it points, and pointing it away from a source costs real
signal even when almost all of that signal has scattered. A module facing the
lake floor is a poor detector of a flash above it at any distance in this
range.

## A laser flash in three clusters {#sec-baikal-laser}

The Baikal-GVD calibration laser emits at $532\,\mathrm{nm}$ with a pulse
energy of $0.37\,\mathrm{mJ}$ through a diffuser designed to make the
emission isotropic, in about $1\,\mathrm{ns}$. At that wavelength a photon
carries $hc/\lambda=3.734\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm J$, so the pulse is

$$
N_\gamma=\frac{0.37\times10^{-3}}{3.734\times10^{-19}}
=9.91\times10^{14}\ \text{photons},
$$

consistent with the $\sim10^{15}$ quoted for the source.

The array is three clusters of the published Baikal-GVD layout: eight strings
each, one central and seven at $60\,\mathrm m$, $36$ modules per string at
$15\,\mathrm m$ spacing between $750$ and $1275\,\mathrm m$ depth, with the
clusters $250\,\mathrm m$ apart; $864$ modules in total. The laser sits on a
string at the centroid, at mid-depth. Modules face the lake floor.

::: {.callout-important}
The water is the repository's synthetic near-Baikal medium, which is
specified at $450\,\mathrm{nm}$, while the laser is a $532\,\mathrm{nm}$
source. This run therefore pairs a real photon yield with synthetic optics.
It demonstrates the method at a realistic scale; it is not a prediction for
Baikal-GVD, and the absorption length of the synthetic medium
($14.3\,\mathrm m$) is shorter than published Baikal values near
$480\,\mathrm{nm}$ ($20$–$25\,\mathrm m$), so it is pessimistic about range.
:::

Converting to photoelectrons uses an effective photocathode area of
$530\,\mathrm{cm}^2$ and a quantum efficiency of $0.20$. No published
quantum efficiency at $532\,\mathrm{nm}$ was found for this module — the
figure usually quoted, $\approx35\%$, is the peak near $400\,\mathrm{nm}$ —
so $0.20$ is an explicit input, and every photoelectron count below scales
linearly with it.

![Plan view of the three clusters and the per-module signal against
distance.](../cache-baikal/figures/cluster-response.png){#fig-cluster width=100%}

With the full pulse and no attenuator, $469$ of the $864$ modules are above
one photoelectron and $592$ above a tenth, the furthest of them at $225$ and
$253\,\mathrm m$ from the flash. The three clusters see comparable numbers —
$158$, $156$ and $155$ modules above one photoelectron — since the laser sits
at their centroid.

What the orders do with distance is the physically interesting part:

| distance | 0 scattering | 1 scattering | $\ge2$ scattering |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| $80$–$120\,\mathrm m$ | $0.145$ | $0.273$ | $0.581$ |
| $120$–$160\,\mathrm m$ | $0.071$ | $0.182$ | $0.748$ |
| $160$–$200\,\mathrm m$ | $0.035$ | $0.114$ | $0.851$ |
| $200$–$250\,\mathrm m$ | $0.018$ | $0.069$ | $0.913$ |
| $250$–$283\,\mathrm m$ | $0.007$ | $0.037$ | $0.956$ |

Beyond about $150\,\mathrm m$ the signal is almost entirely multiply
scattered light — and, by @sec-om-maps, multiply scattered light that still
arrives from the direction of the laser. The unscattered component is gone
not because it was scattered away but because it is attenuated by the full
$\mu_t$ while the scattered component only pays $\mu_a$ along a slightly
longer path.

Two accuracy boundaries apply to this table, and both are measured rather
than assumed. The total charge stops being trustworthy where it falls to
about $10^{-15}$ per square metre per emitted photon: the first unphysical
(negative) component appears at $299.6\,\mathrm m$, where the signal is
$2.4\times10^{-3}$ photoelectrons. All $703$ modules above $10^{-2}$
photoelectrons lie inside that boundary and none of them shows a negative
component. The individual moments fail earlier than their sum: the
first-order mean arrival cosine leaves $[0,1]$ beyond $228\,\mathrm m$, which
is why @fig-arrival stops at $225\,\mathrm m$. Nothing in the table above is
quoted past $283\,\mathrm m$.

At full power the modules nearest the laser are driven far beyond any usable
dynamic range, which is why the real calibration system includes attenuators
between the laser and the diffuser. The interesting quantity is not the peak
but the reach: how far the flash stays above one photoelectron, and what
fraction of that signal is scattered rather than ballistic.

The point of the cache is what it costs to ask. Building it took
$181\,\mathrm s$ once, for $102$ exact distances across three bands. Reading
all $864$ modules out of it then took

| module model | acceptance degrees | query, $864$ modules | per module |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| ideal isotropic | $0$ | $5.3\,\mathrm{ms}$ | $6.1\,\mu\mathrm s$ |
| hemispherical $(1+x)/2$ | $1$ | $4.9\,\mathrm{ms}$ | $5.7\,\mu\mathrm s$ |
| bare cosine $\max(x,0)$ | $364$ | $243\,\mathrm{ms}$ | $261\,\mu\mathrm s$ |

against $0.091\,\mathrm s$ for one direct solve at one module with the same
settings, measured on eight sampled modules. For the smooth acceptance that
is a factor of about $1.6\times10^{4}$; for the kinked one, still about
$350$. The cache pays for itself after roughly two thousand module
evaluations, or — since the build is per medium and per settings, not per
event — after the second flash.

The asymmetry between the two acceptances is the point made in
@sec-om-isotropic, now with numbers: what a query costs is set by the angular
bandwidth of the detector model, because the multipole sum stops where the
acceptance coefficients stop. A module described by a smooth curve is two
orders of magnitude cheaper to evaluate than one described with a hard
cut-off, and the hard cut-off is usually the less physical of the two.
